title: The People Who Built AI Are Sounding the Alarm. Schools Should Be Listening.
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek argues that school leaders racing to adopt AI should weigh the warnings of the researchers who built it. He recounts the 2024 Right to Warn letter, the dissolution of OpenAI's Superalignment team, and departures such as Jan Leike and Daniel Kokotajlo, who say safety has taken a backseat to commercial pressure. He pairs this with school-specific evidence: RAND data on rapid classroom adoption with little training or policy, Center for Democracy and Technology findings that AI makes students feel less connected to teachers, and a Brookings study concluding that current risks outweigh benefits. His recommendations are to slow down, write AI policy, teach AI literacy, protect human relationships and listen to the insiders. He is explicit that this is not a call for a ban but for conditions-based, intentional use.
points: The pressure to adopt AI quickly comes from vendors rather than evidence, and the Brookings review found real benefits only when AI is narrow, tied to vetted content and guided by strong pedagogy.
Adoption is outpacing guardrails: only half of teachers have had any AI training and 60% of schools and districts have no generative AI guidance at all.
Students feeling less connected to teachers because of classroom AI is treated as a warning sign, since relationships with caring adults matter most to learning and wellbeing.
AI literacy should teach students that generative AI is a commercial product with financial incentives, not an oracle.
The better question for schools is under what conditions AI is good for students and how to protect them when it is not, rather than how to integrate AI into everything.
quotes: They were the researchers who helped build the very systems now being marketed to our schools. Their message was blunt: AI companies have strong financial incentives to avoid meaningful oversight, and the internal safety culture at these organizations has eroded under commercial pressure.

A 2025 RAND survey found that 54% of students and 53% of core subject teachers used AI for school — increases of more than 15 percentage points in just two years. But professional development and policy have barely budged. Only 50% of teachers have received even a single training session on AI, and 60% of U.S. schools and districts have no generative AI guidance whatsoever.

The Brookings study found real benefits only when AI is used narrowly, integrated with vetted content, and guided by strong pedagogy. Wholesale adoption without guardrails isn’t innovation. It’s negligence.

Students need to understand that generative AI is a product built by companies with financial incentives — not an oracle of truth. They need to know how these systems are trained, what biases they carry, and why even their creators can’t fully predict their behavior.

The whistleblowers aren’t telling us AI is worthless. They’re telling us the people building it are cutting corners, and that the rest of us need to be more careful than the companies themselves have been willing to be.

We owe our students something better than blind enthusiasm or blind fear. We owe them adults who did the homework, asked the hard questions, and made sure the technology in their classrooms was serving them — not the other way around.
